## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kokilajātaka* (Ja 331), also titled *Kokālikajātaka*, is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [Anandajoti 2010]. According to its traditional frame, the Buddha related this story while residing at the Jetavana monastery in reference to the monk Kokālika (or Kokalika), with its introductory narrative shared with the *Takkarikajātaka*. The core narrative illustrates the perils of ill-timed utterance: a young cuckoo reared in secret by a foster mother crow prematurely betrays its identity by crying out before it is grown, prompting the crow to peck it to death and throw it from the nest [Anandajoti 2010]. The teaching is summarized in verse (beginning *Yo ve kāle asampatte...*), underscoring the importance of correct, timely, and restrained speech [Anandajoti 2010].

In terms of text reuse and parallels, the canonical verse material corresponds directly to the commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, automatic cross-language alignments generated by DharmaNexus indicate textual and gnomic affinities between the verses of Ja 331 and Buddhist and Indian wisdom literature preserved in Tibetan translation, including the *Udānavarga* (D4099) and the *Cāṇakyarājanītiśāstra* (D4334) [DharmaNexus].
